articles.title: Flu: a public health crisis
articles.content: LAST fall, after many years, my wife, our daughter and I decided to get flu shots. The decision wasn’t popular with our nine-year-old, who doesn’t like having her skin punctured, but we thought that, given the smog season and the health disruptions we faced every winter in Lahore, it was worth the trouble and expense. And it was. Last winter, we had far fewer bouts of illness, despite the smog highs; when we did have symptoms, they were much milder and recovery much faster. My wife and I lost fewer days at work, and our daughter was able to go to school most days. We also relied much less on cough syrups, antibiotics, and similar medications. It is almost that time of the year again. Flu shots should be available soon, if they aren’t already. Since influenza mutates significantly, the flu vaccine has to be updated often, and shots have to be taken every year. Despite this inconvenience, they are worth it. But it seems they are not very popular or widely available in Pakistan. We had to ask around and find clinics where we could get a flu shot. A muscular injection, they should be available at most, if not all, pharmacies. Last year, our shot cost around Rs3,000 per head. So, they can be expensive for many households, but, given the cost-benefit, the state should make them available to vulnerable populations free of charge. It is very much a public health issue. The evidence from other countries is clear. The return on investment is indeed significant. Flu shots save the lives of vulnerable people: children, older populations, and people with compromised health and co-morbidities. Hospitalisations are fewer, and symptoms are less severe and more manageable when people fall sick. Even for the healthy, flu shots can collectively save millions of work hours. Children miss school less. And flu shots also create herd immunity. For the cost, could one ask for more? In the UK, all children are given flu vaccines free of charge. These are administered in September. Since most or all children are in school in the UK, schools administer the vaccine, which is efficient and effective. For children, there is even a version that can be squirted up the nose, so an injection is not the only option. I am sure children are quite happy with that. It is a story of neglect. There is no public effort to promote flu vaccination. The elderly also have access to free shots, as do any adults whose health systems might be compromised: diabetes, immune disorders, etc. The National Health Service administers the shots. This is a large campaign and can have significant waiting times, but it gets done. For other adults, shots are available at most pharmacies for £10 to £25 per shot. Given the protection the shot offers, many adults do get them every year. This helps the UK build significant herd immunity. Given Pakistan’s higher smog levels, elevated child malnutrition, and the fact that about one-third of the adult population is diabetic, one would think that flu shots would be even more important for us and treated as a public health issue. Of course, if we had national campaigns for flu shots, they would be organised differently from those in other countries. Not all of our children are in schools, and we do not have a comprehensive national health service. So, we will need to have a network involving public health institutions (basic health and above) and Lady Health Workers and Visitors. Availability through private clinics, hospitals, and pharmacies would also need to be ensured. Some mechanism would have to be designed to ensure that vulnerable and deserving populations have easy access to the vaccine at low or no cost (BISP and similar programmes with large outreach). This won’t be easy for our health authorities. But maybe the lessons from Covid vaccinations can be useful here. Sadly, as usual, it is a story of neglect. There is no public effort to promote flu vaccination. It does not even seem to be on the agenda. Even with visible rising health costs from increasing smog, office and school closures, and other disruptions, there has been no effort to address the issue. Individuals and families largely bear the cost of ill health. If a child falls ill, the child bears the health cost, and the family pays for care. If flu spreads through an infected child, the increased cost is now borne by other children and households. If an adult falls ill and misses work, the cost is again mostly borne by the person, his or her family, and the individual business or workplace. The state does not bear any costs. There is no realisation of how much this costs society and the economy as a whole. This is something the state should worry about, but since it is not an explicit cost, it does not. If costs rise for businesses, revenues and profits decline; households bear higher costs — all of this is reflected in national output and performance figures. The impact on health, longevity and morbidity is separate from this. Sadly, the state does not care much about them either. With smog expectations the way they are, we are likely to experience another tough winter. Considering the impact on children and adults, and keeping in view the days missed at school because of ill health, and even school closures, a large campaign to vaccinate schoolchildren and vulnerable populations makes sense. Sadly, since this requires significant preparation, we are likely to miss this season again. Maybe, next year it will be different. The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
articles.author: Faisal Bari

articles.title: Bank domination
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S financial system is heavily bank-centric. Commercial banks account for over 80 per cent of total financial-sector assets. In a mature financial system, household and corporate savings flow through multiple competing channels — capital markets, pension funds, insurance companies, asset managers and private equity. But in Pakistan, many of the institutions that should compete with banks are themselves economically and financially connected to them. What appears to be institutional diversity is, to a large extent, concentration masquerading as diversification. Banks dominate for many reasons. They possess advantages their competitors cannot easily replicate: large capital bases, extensive branch and distribution networks, long-standing ties with government, customer trust built through decades of deposit-taking, and access to millions of small deposits through everyday transaction accounts. This gives them balance-sheet strength, scale and a low-cost funding advantage. Their established relationships with borrowers, ability to demand collateral and capacity to monitor credit also make them natural intermediaries. These advantages are barriers to entry for competing financial institutions. But the most important explanation is the government’s persistent financing needs. Commercial banks have become the easiest channel through which government finances its fiscal deficit. Today, some 62pc of banking assets comprise government securities, while lending to the private sector accounts for a mere 22pc. Banks have become primary financiers of the state rather than intermediaries channelling savings into productive private investment. The incentives are obvious. Government securities offer double-digit, effectively risk-free returns. Lending to private businesses requires assessment of credit risk, documentation, collateral, monitoring. Why create capability to underwrite bonds, financial instruments or support new equity listings when there is an attractive return on financing government with little effort? As long as government continues to rely on banks to finance its deficit, banks will remain the dominant and highly profitable powerhouses in the financial architecture. The state reinforces this dominance. It borrows heavily from banks, operates National Savings, owns financial institutions, influences development finance, etc. An independent financial institution is not only competing against banks, it is competing against the state itself. Commercial banks have become the easiest channel through which government finances its fiscal deficit. The weakness of capital markets reinforces this structure. Stock-market participation is low — account holders represent less than 0.5pc of the population. Households prefer cash, bank deposits, real estate and physical gold, reflecting limited financial literacy as well as a historical mistrust of market volatility. Corporate sector listing on the PSX or issuing corporate bonds requires compliance of SECP regulations involving extensive disclosure, auditing, corporate-governance requirements, credit ratings, which is time-consuming and expensive. Corporate debt consequently accounts for less than 3pc of Pakistan’s debt market. For most businesses, borrowing from a bank is faster and easier — secured through a bilateral relationship with a banker — than raising capital from the market. For large corporates that tend to be family-controlled businesses there is little incentive to list. A bank loan only requires a discussion with a bank official, while listing also brings exposure to tax and regulatory authorities. Retained earnings and bank borrowing therefore remain the preferred sources of corporate finance. Institutional investors that could provide an alternative source of long-term capital are underdeveloped. Pakistan lacks a mandatory, broad-based pension system. Existing pension arrangements revolve largely around government employees and are predominantly unfunded and pay-as-you-go. Pension and insurance assets therefore remain minuscule relative to GDP. Investment restrictions further constrain them, with public-sector pension and insurance institutions required to place much of their funds in government securities or bank deposits. Pakistan’s regulators have been reasonably successful in ensuring that banks remain solvent, liquid and systemically safe. But the same regulatory architecture has not succeeded in creating institutions capable of competing with them. Large capital requirements may be justified for institutions taking substantial risks with other people’s money. But applying requirements designed for banks to specialist institutions creates prohibitive fixed costs. Mutual funds illustrate the problem. Non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) are legally prohibited from taking demand or retail deposits. They must, instead, persuade savers to voluntarily invest with them or raise capital through equity or borrow from banks at commercial interest rates. Products connecting banking and capital markets require clearances from both SBP and SECP, creating regulatory silos and slowing innovation in financial products. A process intended to protect consumers can, if poorly crafted, protect incumbents instead. Good regulation must distinguish between prudential requirements that protect customers and systemic stability, and high fixed regulatory costs that prevent new institutions from entering the market. Also, SBP’s discount window and emergency liquidity facilities are exclusively available to banks, while NBFIs operate within a fragmented and evolving framework without comparable institutional support. Banking regulation has enjoyed greater stability and predictability over decades, whereas the regulatory framework for NBFIs has been repeatedly redrafted. Unsurprisingly, banks have responded rationally. Rather than compete with NBFIs, they have established or acquired them. The largest asset-management companies and mutual funds are not extensions of the bank’s balance sheet, they are overwhelmingly owned or controlled by banks. Their apparent independence hides their integration into the banking system. These institutions will, in the absence of sufficiently deep corporate bond markets, take corporate or household savings, invest them in Treasury bills, government-sponsored Sukuks or bank deposits-instruments that already exist — and channel much of that money back into the banking system. Ownership, distribution, funding and investment decisions remain concentrated within the same financial groups. Pakistan’s financial system is therefore bank-dominated not simply because banks are efficient or because savers prefer them. It is bank-dominated because the state’s financing needs, corporate structures and the regulatory architecture have prevented alternative channels of financial intermediation from acquiring scale and independence. The challenge is not to license more NBFIs while leaving these structural incentives unscathed. We require a function-based, competitively neutral financial system in which regulation protects risks of financial activities rather than the institutional boundaries between banks and NBFIs. Until then, Pakistan will continue to have many financial institutions but essentially one dominant player in the financial system — the banks. The writer is a former governor of the State Bank.
articles.author: Shahid Kardar

articles.title: Political order
articles.content: MAN’S superiority over creation lies in his faculty of creative knowledge, ie, the capacity to discover the laws of, and thus achieve mastery over, nature, or, in Quranic terminology, “to know the names of all things”, and then use this mastery under the human initiative to create a just political world order. Endowed with choice and charged with responsibility, man is a bearer of ‘Trust’ under whose weight the entire universe chafed. He assumed the task which the heavens, despite their heights, the earth despite its vastness, and the mountains, despite their firmness, shrank from undertaking. This task involves fulfilling the primordial covenant: to establish a just world order, since the challenge God gave man at creation was to create a sociopolitical order that reflects the equality all people share in the eyes of God. It was to orient the forces of history towards a just social order rather than to compromise with them under the cover of secularism. Hence, for Islam, politics is through and through a moral endeavour to accomplish the task. The Quranic idea of ‘fauz’ (success) or ‘khusran’ (failure) is rooted in executing the same task, since it is the quality of the political process through which civilisations rise and fall. The Quran, in its coherent unity, shows that it is a troika of religious, political, and mercantile elites that manoeuvres the materials of history towards their vested interests. And when exploitation reaches its critical point, the whole of society or civilisation is mowed down. When the Quran talks about the death of individuals like Pharaoh, Qarun and Haman, it is showing the self-destructiveness of the way of life of a society or civilisation. The remedy lies in building a just sociopolitical order, since societies built on unbelief may survive, but unjust ones may not. Now, because injustice is often rooted in socioeconomic disequilibrium and grave fiscal malpractices can lead to socioeconomic suicide (4:29-32), the Quran makes monotheism-based socioeconomic reforms the linchpin of its moral programme. Therefore, Islam, since its very inception, was socio-politically geared to uproot the corrupt socioeconomic structures of Persia and Byzantium and to build anew, to inject fresh blood into the veins of a decrepit and decadent humanity. In Islam politics is through and through a moral endeavour. Islam views power as a means to an end, not an end in itself, as prayer and zakat are instruments of socioeconomic equality. Implementing them in letter and spirit required political power, so the Prophet (PBUH) felt duty-bound to build a state based on an ethical sociopolitical order. Hence, man is a moral political being with ibada as his purpose of creation — which means to know the will of God and implement it in life, and to restore moral order in individual and social life to redeem the balance of history. The Quran constituted an egalitarian community, with equal rights for all to participate in or lead the execution of the task through shura, or mutual consultation. The community’s internal conduct was based on active goodwill and cooperation with no trace of elitism. Externally, it kept inviting the religious others to share the burden of building a world moral order. It fared well and was blessed with political control of Arabia, eventually expanding into parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. However, later, with the onset and patronage of dictatorship, Sufism Hellenised almost every bit of the faith. In the long run, this development resulted in the colonisation of Muslim Asia and Africa by Western po-wers. At this critical juncture, Syed Jamal al-Din Afghani rediscovered the Quran’s moral political vision. He proposed building an Islamic republic across a wide region of Central Asia and the Muslim-majority areas of northwest India to realise Islam’s sociopolitical ideals. He amply fired the imagination of Iqbal and Ali Shariati. The former conceived the idea of Pakistan, and the latter paved the way for the Islamic Revolution in Iran. Today, the Muslim world has either succumbed to secular structures or theocratic modes. The realisation of the Quran’s moral political vision that seeks just socioeconomic and democratic organisation of society seems like a distant dream. The Quran hardly demands military conquests which could stand in the way of the prospects of the socio-democratic organisation of society. What the vision needs is a tract of land with a just political order whose fragrance may be smelt in the world around and which, in the long run, is destined to create a just world order. Does such a realisation prevail anywhere in the Muslim world?
articles.author: Ghulam Shabbir

articles.title: Terror forever
articles.content: THE 9/11 attacks happened 25 years ago, ushering in a new epoch. The so-called global war on terror was launched by the Bush administration a few days later, and Washington has wreaked havoc across the globe ever since. The majority of the world’s states have followed the US lead by making the prosecution and hunting down of ‘terrorists’ their primary raison d’être. Ideological apparatuses, including the culture industry, have indoctrinated generations of young and old alike into believing that ‘terror’ is ubiquitous and that the state must be endlessly empowered to snuff it out, even at the cost of basic liberties. Pakistan was one of the major staging grounds of the ‘war on terror’, facilitating both the US invasion and occupation of Afghanistan whilst also launching innumerable military operations on its own soil. A plethora of ‘anti-terrorist’ laws have been promulgated since 2001, the scope of which is growing wider. While these instruments are deployed to clamp down on all forms of dissent and popular political mobilisation, the insurgencies and other forms of political violence that ostensibly should have been curbed by the state’s various ‘counterterrorist’ initiatives have only become more intense. Beneath the surface, a global military-industrial complex profits endlessly from the West’s totalitarian regime. Washington has thrown $8 trillion at various wars since 2001, a significant chunk of which has been pocketed by private defence contractors integrated with the deep state. In Pakistan, too, the ‘war on terror’ inaugurated a host of opportunities for state functionaries and private contractors to mint money. The policing of dissent is paralleled by Big Tech’s power. Today, we are at another crossroads. With the rise of Big Tech to the apex of global capitalism, the nexus of state and private capital has morphed into a behemoth without historical precedent. The discourse around ‘terrorism’ expanded some years ago in conjunction with the dramatic transformations of cultural, economic and political life provoked by digitalisation. Terms like ‘cyberterrorism/‘cybersecurity’ and ‘fifth-generation war’ reflect the evolution of a political idiom that both incorporates the logics of the war on terror and extends well beyond it. The policing of dissent by the state and aligned propagandists in the digital lifeworld is paralleled by the immense power of Big Tech companies to access, share and manipulate data. Earlier this week, a whistleblower resigned from Anthropic, warning that AI development is being allowed to spiral into an existential threat to humanity. Anthropic’s Claude tool has already shown its destructive capabilities at the outset of the war on Iran. Edward Snowden told us what was coming as early as 2013. Despite their claims of being pro-market libertarians, billionaires like Peter Thiel and Elon Musk are buttressing the state’s immense coercive and surveillance capacities. They view humanity as a plaything that is, at best, ‘saved’ and, at worst, sacrificed in the interests of landing on Mars or crafting more ‘intelligent’ species. Quite aside from hyperbolic claims that an AI-triggered extinction event is around the corner, the unbridled pursuit of power and profit by Big Tech alongside the contemporary state’s unlimited quest for social control must surely trouble anyone concerned with the age-old quest for human emancipation. Even non-human life is at stake. At a time when climate breakdown events are playing out with ever greater frequency and intensity, states everywhere are bending over backwards to build huge data centres to serve Big Tech’s interests by guaranteeing enormous and uninterrupted supplies of electricity and water. The US state and Silicon Valley billionaires are the primary protagonists of the contemporary militarised capitalist order. But we cannot be seduced by blind-faith arguments that there are ‘good’ states — not least of them our own — and ‘green’ capitalisms that do not conform to the overarching logic of the system. We need, instead, to learn the lessons from the ‘war on terror’ and stop being cheerleaders for an even more sinister and unhinged digitalised fusion of state and corporate power that will shape our present and future. A critical mass in Pakistan continues to speak truth to the militarised ruling class over its whittling away of the few civil liberties we still possess, including in the digital domain, whilst also resisting resource grabs and dispossession. The challenge, however, is outlined every time an episode of ‘terrorism’ is capitalised upon by the state to whip up a nationalist frenzy in which all good sense is abandoned. If the global totalitarian regime’s march is to be halted, we must coalesce around an anti-capitalist ideological politics rooted in working people and nature. And soon. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
articles.author: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar

articles.title: After Sept 11
articles.content: A QUARTER of a century since the Sept 11 terrorist attacks, the world continues to feel the effects of that epochal event. The US response to the attacks on its soil went beyond a counterterrorism operation. It metastasised into a sprawling imperial ‘crusade’ that laid to waste countries that had nothing to do with the terrorists who had hijacked the American airliners. In fact, the US misadventure in Iran is a continuation of these flawed policies. Today, the world is no safer from religiously inspired terrorism than it was 25 years ago, reflecting the futility of the American-led ‘global war on terror’ and its modern-day iterations. Soon after the attacks, Muslims, including Arabs, in the US faced intense discrimination. Matters may have improved in some respects; after all, New York City, which was the epicentre of the terrorist attacks, today haselected a Muslim mayor. But conversely, Islamophobia in the US is currently at historic levels, spiking after thelaunch of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in 2023. The current US administration has contributed to this bias, with many of President Donald Trump’s close confidantes spewing reprehensible views. Big Tech, too, has played a significant role in mainstreaming anti-Muslim hate across the larger West. In the field of foreign policy, little has changed. Post-Sept 11, Washington launched invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq. In the first instance, after a two-decade nation-building experiment, the Americansbeat a hasty retreat, leaving Kabul to the Afghan Taliban who returned to power. In Iraq, the US occupation resulted in a vicious sectarian war, which paved the way for the rise of the self-styled Islamic State group. IS was arguably even more brutal than Al Qaeda, the outfit the Americans had sought to crush for carrying out the Sept 11 attacks. Though its abilities stand diminished today, IS continues to threaten global security, putting a question mark over America’s transnational counterterrorism campaign. Following George W. Bush, even ‘liberal’ presidents, such as the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Barack Obama, backed regime-change operations in Libya and Syria. Today, both remain broken states. Despite some bitter lessons, the current US president champions American exceptionalism, and violates the sovereignty of other nations in pursuit of his nebulous goals. Where the Iranian misadventure is concerned, the reasons cited for Washington’s aggression have kept changing. America’s ‘war on terror’, in fact, spawned even more lethal terrorist groups, while leaving in its wake gulags such as Guantánamo Bay and Abu Ghraib, alongside populations in several Muslim countries grappling with the residue of collapsed states. The post-Sept 11 period offers lessons in imperial overreach, and how not to fight terrorism. But as its actions continue to show, the US has learnt no lessons at all.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Towards dystopia
articles.content: FIRST, AI became capable. It began demonstrating surprising capabilities in generating text, images, code and analysis. Then it became autonomous. It started using tools, navigating systems and working around set objectives. Now, it is getting too difficult to control. Experts warn it has become difficult to understand how AI systems arrive at the answers they provide, and say their behaviour is becoming harder to predict. AI has also been acquiring capabilities that could be dangerous: the ability to launch cyberattacks, for example, or compress a lifetime’s worth of research onto a machine, or the ability to replicate autonomously, or to coordinate behaviour with other AI systems in pursuit of common goals. Reality is now starting to resemble the beginning of a dystopian science fiction novel but, instead of applying the brakes and taking a moment to understand where the near-exponential improvements in AI are leading humanity, tech companies and their leaders are becoming increasingly invested in what has started to resemble an AI arms race. It is an arms race that some researchers say could eventually drive all of humanity to extinction. A researcher at Anthropic, one of the foremost companies in AI development, resigned this week, citing concerns that his company and its competitors are not acting responsibly enough. Jacob Coxon, the researcher in question, believes both Anthropic and its rival OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, are more obsessed with besting each other and their global competition than worrying about what safety risks the extremely advanced AI models they are releasing pose to the public. It bears mentioning that, this summer, OpenAI’s AI models broke out of their testing environment and coordinated a multi-step cyberattack targeting Hugging Face, an AI development platform. The incident prompted widespread concerns about AI agents ‘going rogue’ and potentially causing real-world harm. More recent disclosures suggest that AI agents from multiple labs, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta, have broken out of containment far more frequently than originally reported. Taken as a whole, this presents a worrying picture, but there may yet be time to act. Instead of going to war, AI companies must recognise the imminent danger from unchecked development and collaborate on establishing a ceiling on AI capabilities till they figure out how to control what they are creating. The future of humanity itself might be at stake.
articles.author: Editorial
